newsitem.title: INDIA: India's new PM set to clinch confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: India's new PM set to clinch confidence vote.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's new United Front alliance government was set to win a trust vote on Tuesday and looked certain to clinch eventual parliamentary approval for a landmark budget.

Gujral, who succeeded ousted prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Monday after the previous United Front government was voted from power 10 days ago, sought a fresh vote of confidence, promising an administration by consultation.
"The government will strive for a national consensus on foreign policy and economic issues," Gujral told the lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha.
The vote, initially set for about 1230 GMT, was delayed by lengthy debate but was still expected to be held on Tuesday.

The Congress party, which triggered Deve Gowda's fall after withdrawing its make-or-break support for his 10-month-old government, promised to back Gujral for the remaining four years of the Lok Sabha, but with conditions.

Former finance minister Manmohan Singh, the Congress party's economic policy advisor, told Reuters that Gujral's tenure hinged on the success of a coordination committee set up by the two quarrelling allies to sort out policy differences.
The beginning appeared promising.
Singh said Congress would not seek any changes in the budget proposals for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) presented by former United Front finance minister P. Chidambaram.
"Reports that we are seeking to change the budget are wrong and baseless," Singh said. "I see no problem in the passage of the budget."
But he said economic policy was one of the key issues to be discussed by the Congress-United Front coordination committee, headed by Gujral and Congress president Sitaram Kesri.

"I think the government will last as long as the coordination mechanism works, and I hope it works for four years," Singh said moments before Gujral moved the motion in parliament to seek a trust vote.
The rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), however, said the new government would be short-lived.
"There is already a serious rift over Chidambaram," former BJP finance minister Jaswant Singh told Reuters.

He was referring to the decision by Chidambaram's regional Tamil Maanila Congress party to stay out of the government after its leader G.K. Moopanar was passed over in the leadership tussle last week.
BJP leaders said they would oppose passage of Chidambaram's finance bill, supported by the new government and due to be taken up for discussion on April 30.
"I don't think this government will last beyond 1997," former BJP interior minister Murli Manohar Joshi said.
The centre-left ruling coalition was originally cobbled together with Congress support in June last year to oust a 12-day-old government headed by BJP leader Atal Behari Vajpayee.
When Congress withdrew support to Deve Gowda, it accused him of not keeping the BJP contained.
But the 15-party alliance under Gujral, a 77-year-old Marxist turned social democrat, was expected easily to prove its parliamentary majority after patching up relations with Congress.
Gujral and Deve Gowda belong to the left-leaning Janata Dal party, the biggest single constituent in the alliance.
The BJP controls 193 votes in the 545-seat lower house of parliament. Congress has 140 and the United Front 178.
